claim: Brackets are marginal; 2025 single brackets $11,925/$48,475/$103,350; $60,000 taxable owes $8,114, avg 13.5%.

edits.old: Federal income tax is charged in layers called brackets. Each bracket's rate applies only to the slice of taxable income that falls inside it, not to the whole amount. Moving into a higher bracket therefore raises the tax on the next dollar earned, not on the dollars already taxed at lower rates. The rate on the last dollar is the marginal rate; total tax divided by total income is the average rate, and it is always lower than the marginal rate.

claim: Rent vs own: owning builds equity slowly, has transaction/maintenance costs; early sellers may gain no equity; 2007-2012 declines.

edits.old: Renting Versus Owning
edits.new: Home Equity

edits.old: The rent-or-own question is a comparison of two cost streams under uncertainty. Owning builds equity - the home's value minus the mortgage balance - but slowly at first, because early payments are mostly interest, and equity also moves with market prices. It carries transaction costs at purchase and sale, plus maintenance and repairs. Renting avoids those costs and preserves the option to move, at the price of building no equity. Calculators that compare the two depend heavily on assumed price growth.
edits.new: Home equity is the home's market value minus what is still owed on the mortgage. It grows two ways: as payments reduce the loan balance and as the home's price rises. Early payments are mostly interest, so the first route is slow at first, and the second can run in reverse when prices fall. Selling also costs money, so after a short stay the transaction costs can leave an owner with no more equity than at purchase.

edits.old: The CFPB's guide notes that someone who sells within the first few years may end up with no more equity than they started with after paying the transaction costs, and that when prices fell between 2007 and 2012 many owners lost some or all of their equity. Owners also bear repairs a landlord would otherwise cover, so the comparison must include more than a rent check against a mortgage payment.
edits.new: An illustrative buyer puts $30,000 down on a $300,000 home. If the price stays flat, 3 years of payments on the 30-year, $270,000 loan at 6.5 percent cut the balance by about $9,700; selling costs of $10,000 would leave about $29,700, slightly less than was put in. The CFPB notes that when prices fell between 2007 and 2012, many owners lost some or all of their equity.

edits.old: Errors in a credit report can lower a score and raise borrowing costs, and federal law gives the consumer a right to dispute them. A dispute goes to the credit reporting company, in writing with copies of supporting documents, and often also to the company that supplied the information, called the furnisher. The reporting company must investigate, forward the dispute and evidence to the furnisher, and report the result back; it may decline only disputes it reasonably finds frivolous.

The reporting company must investigate, forward the dispute and evidence to the furnisher, and report the result back; it may decline only disputes it reasonably finds frivolous.

claim: Compound interest defined; SEC $100 at 5%: $105, $110.25, >$162 at 10 yrs, ~$340 at 25 yrs.

edits.old: Compound Interest
edits.new: Regular Deposits Over Time

edits.old: Compounding is interest earning interest. After the first period, the credited interest joins the principal, and the next period's interest is calculated on the larger sum. Early on the effect is barely visible - a few cents of interest on interest. But the extra amount itself compounds, so growth accelerates over time, and the final balance depends far more on how long the money was left than on the size of any single year's gain. The same mathematics works against a borrower who carries a balance.
edits.new: Compounding also works on money added along the way. Each deposit starts earning interest once it is in the account, so a steady monthly amount builds a balance with two parts: the deposits themselves and the interest they have earned. Deposits made early have the longest to compound, so the interest share of the balance keeps growing the longer the schedule runs. The SEC's compound interest calculator asks for the same inputs: a starting amount, a monthly contribution, a number of years, a rate, and how often interest compounds.

edits.old: The SEC's classroom example: $100 earning 5 percent a year becomes $105 after 1 year and $110.25 after 2, the extra 25 cents being interest on the first year's $5. Left alone, the $100 grows to more than $162 after 10 years and to almost $340 after 25 years, without another cent deposited. Nearly all of the later gain is interest on earlier interest.
edits.new: An illustrative  a month at 5 percent a year, compounded monthly, grows to about ,500 after 10 years, of which ,000 is deposits and about ,500 is interest. After 30 years the balance is about ,200 on ,000 of deposits, so interest makes up more than half of it. The rate is an assumption; real returns vary from year to year.

claim: Inflation erodes purchasing power; FOMC 2% PCE longer-run goal; at 2% prices double in ~35 years.

edits.old: Inflation and Purchasing Power
edits.new: A Guaranteed Doubling

edits.old: Inflation is a general rise in prices, which is the same thing as a fall in what a unit of money buys. A savings balance that stays fixed in dollars shrinks in purchasing power every year prices rise. Because it compounds like interest, even a low rate matters over decades. Central banks aim for a low, stable rate so that households and businesses can plan; the U.S. Federal Reserve states its objective as a specific number measured by a specific price index.
edits.new: A Series EE savings bond is a U.S. Treasury bond that earns a fixed rate of interest for up to 30 years. Treasury adds one promise on top of the rate: the bond will double in value 20 years after purchase, and if the fixed rate has not done that by then, Treasury adds the difference at 20 years. Because the guarantee arrives only at that date, how long the bond is held matters as much as the rate printed on it.

edits.old: The Federal Open Market Committee judges that inflation of 2 percent over the longer run, measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with its mandate for price stability and maximum employment. At exactly that pace, prices double in roughly 35 years, so $100 set aside at the start buys about what $50 did.
edits.new: EE bonds issued from May 1 to October 31, 2026 earn a fixed 2.40 percent. At that rate alone, ,000 would grow to only about ,600 in 20 years, so Treasury makes up the rest to bring it to ,000. Doubling in 20 years works out to roughly 3.5 percent a year, paid in full only to an owner who waits the whole 20 years.

claim: Rule of 72 approximation; claims it overstates at higher rates; 9%->8 yrs, 2%->36 vs 35, 24%->3 vs 3.2.

edits.old: The Rule of 72 is a mental shortcut for compounding: dividing 72 by an annual growth rate gives the approximate number of years for an amount to double. It is an approximation, most accurate for rates in the single digits and steadily less so at higher rates, where it overstates the doubling time. It works in reverse too: dividing 72 by an inflation rate gives roughly how long until money buys half as much. It assumes a constant rate, which real returns rarely deliver.
edits.new: The Rule of 72 is a mental shortcut for compounding: dividing 72 by an annual growth rate gives the approximate number of years for an amount to double. It is an approximation, most accurate for rates near 8 percent; it slightly overstates the doubling time at lower rates and understates it at higher ones. It works in reverse too: dividing 72 by an inflation rate gives roughly how long until money buys half as much. It assumes a constant rate, which real returns rarely deliver.

note: Wrong direction: the rule overstates doubling time below about 8% and understates it above (the card's own 24% case: 3 vs 3.22). Accuracy peaks near 8%, not across single digits. The SEC 9%/8-year example is verified. Partly overlaps Markets rr-003.

edits.old: A useful way to size a cash reserve is in time rather than dollars: how many months of essential spending it would cover if income stopped. Measured that way, the target scales automatically with a household's costs, and it can be built in steps. The CFPB's guidance ties the amount to the person's own history of unexpected expenses and income swings rather than to a universal figure, and notes that a reserve of any size shortens recovery from a shock and reduces reliance on borrowing.

edits.old: Real Return
edits.new: The National Deposit Rate

edits.old: The real return on savings is the interest rate minus the inflation rate: what the balance gains in purchasing power rather than in dollars. A deposit earning less than inflation loses ground even as its balance rises. The FDIC publishes a national deposit rate, the average of what insured banks and credit unions pay on common account types, weighted by each institution's share of deposits, which shows how far typical savings rates sit from the rates on other instruments.
edits.new: The FDIC publishes a national deposit rate for common account types: the average rate paid by insured banks and credit unions for which data is available, weighted by each institution's share of domestic deposits. It is a benchmark for what typical balances earn, not an offer from any institution. Set against inflation, it gives a rough real return - the deposit rate minus the inflation rate - which is negative whenever prices rise faster than the balance grows.

note: Rates match the FDIC August 2026 release (latest). The definition duplicated core ir-003 (real vs nominal rates), so it is refocused on the FDIC national rate, a new concept, and marks the subtraction as approximate.
